strengths: The paper presents an original and practically useful simplification of difficult three-view geometry problems. Generating virtual correspondences from point coordinates allows mature 5-point/6-point and P3P solvers to operate from four real correspondences. The supported calibrated-camera contribution provides the main reason for weak acceptance.

The calibrated results demonstrate a meaningful accuracy–runtime tradeoff. In Table 2, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F achieves PhotoTourism AUC@10 of 70.47 versus 70.54 for 5pt+P3P, while reducing runtime from 105.50 to 75.78 ms. The faster M+R+F variant reaches 69.06 at 30.54 ms and improves both accuracy and runtime over the evaluated homotopy-continuation baseline.

The evaluation is extensive: PhotoTourism and Cambridge Landmarks, two RANSAC frameworks, noise experiments, controlled outlier ratios, and per-scene runtime–accuracy curves. The supplementary evaluation includes all three camera pairs, addressing the main metric’s omission of the second-to-third-camera relationship. These experiments support practical usefulness beyond isolated solver timings.

The main construction is understandable and uses accessible components. Ablations separate virtual-point shifts, filtering, and refinement, with hyperparameters selected on a held-out scene. The manuscript also candidly acknowledges approximation error, scene dependence, and the limited benefit of learning after refinement.
weaknesses: The shared-focal-length contribution is substantially less convincing empirically. In Table 3, 4p3vf(M) obtains AUC@10 of 49.88 at 12.67 ms, compared with 56.79 at 11.72 ms for 6pt+P3P. Even the strongest reported learned variant reaches only 53.56 at 259.63 ms. Focal-length estimation error is not reported, and the low-inlier-ratio advantage is not demonstrated specifically for this extension. The results establish a fast four-point construction more clearly than a practical advantage over the six-point baseline.

The approximation’s operating limits remain under-characterized. Lemma 1 bounds virtual-point epipolar error by a triangle-size quantity, which can be large; it does not bound pose error or establish convergence of refinement. Table 1 and Figure 14 show substantial scene dependence, and the method retains error with noiseless inputs. Since the real-data protocol requires at least 10% overlap, the acknowledged weakness under small overlap is not directly quantified. This limits generalization claims without invalidating the reported calibrated results.

The learned extension adds little demonstrated practical value and has an unresolved technical specification. Table 2 gives nearly identical PhotoTourism AUC@10 for L+R and M+R, 69.88 versus 69.90, while runtime increases from 74.94 to 297.88 ms. Moreover, Equation (2), presented as the training loss, is a signed epipolar residual without a square or absolute value; minimizing it directly does not encourage zero epipolar error. This could be a notation error, but the manuscript does not establish the actual nonnegative training objective.

Reporting and reproducibility issues weaken confidence in auxiliary comparisons. Section 4 says the Nistér oracle performs worse than the proposed oracle, whereas Table 7 and Section 9.7 report the opposite; footnote 6 attributes this reversal to an unspecified RANSAC modification. Table 9 also repeats the M±δ accuracy values and nearly identical runtimes for corresponding L±δ variants, despite the network overhead documented in Table 10. These inconsistencies, together with incomplete specification of numerical RANSAC thresholds and refinement details, obstruct exact reproduction. They are secondary to the supported deterministic contribution, but require clarification.
